# Part 0 · Setup

### Chunk 0.1 · Packages and data (given — just run it)

We start from the cleaned Compustat data of Tutorial 2: industrial format, one row per firm-year, US firms in USD.

```{r chunk_0_1}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

cs <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"),
               col_types = cols(gvkey = col_character(), sic = col_character()),
               guess_max = Inf) |>
  filter(indfmt == "INDL", !is.na(fyear), fic == "USA", curcd == "USD") |>
  arrange(gvkey, fyear, desc(datadate)) |>
  distinct(gvkey, fyear, .keep_all = TRUE)

stopifnot(!any(duplicated(cs[c("gvkey", "fyear")])))
dim(cs)
```

# Part 1 · Concepts and proxies

Every empirical study translates **concepts** (what we want to talk about) into **measures** (what we can observe).
Libby boxes make this translation explicit:

|   | Concept (X) | → | Concept (Y) |
|--------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Conceptual level** | Informativeness of disclosure policy | → | Analyst following |
|  | ↓ *construct validity* |  | ↓ *construct validity* |
| **Operational level** | FAF disclosure score (rating by analysts) | → | Number of analysts with an IBES forecast |
| **Other influences** | firm size, return volatility, earnings–return correlation |  |  |

*Lang and Lundholm (1996).* The weakest link?
The FAF score measures **analysts' perception** of disclosure — and the same group of people (analysts) also produce the outcome.
The authors discuss this themselves (p. 474–475).

**Task A:** Fill in the Libby boxes for the frontier paper, **Huang, Hugon, Zhang and Zheng (2026)**.
Which link worries you most?

|                       | Concept (X) | →   | Concept (Y) |
|-----------------------|-------------|-----|-------------|
| **Conceptual level**  |             | →   |             |
| **Operational level** |             | →   |             |
| **Other influences**  |             |     |             |

Both papers measure the **same concept**, forecast accuracy, with **different proxies**:

- Lang & Lundholm: $-\,|EPS - \text{median forecast}| \,/\, \text{Price}$
- Huang et al.: $-$ PMAFE, the analyst's absolute error divided by the average absolute error of all analysts for that firm

Scaling matters: dividing by price makes firms with low prices look extremely inaccurate.
We see the same problem with our own data in Part 4.

# Part 2 · Descriptive statistics

Descriptive statistics come first in every paper (usually Table 1 or 2).
They tell the reader — and you — what the data look like: how many observations, typical values, spread, extreme values.

### Chunk 2.1 · Build the variables

```{r chunk_2_1}
cs <- cs |>
  mutate(sic1 = str_sub(sic, 1, 1),                 # one-digit industry
         sic2 = str_sub(sic, 1, 2),                 # two-digit industry
         mv   = prcc_f * csho,                      # market value (USD millions)
         roa  = ib / at,                            # return on assets
         eps  = ib / csho)                          # earnings per share

## Lagged values within each firm (previous fiscal year)
cs <- cs |>
  arrange(gvkey, fyear) |>
  group_by(gvkey) |>
  mutate(eps_lag   = if_else(lag(fyear) == fyear - 1, lag(eps), NA_real_),
         price_lag = if_else(lag(fyear) == fyear - 1, lag(prcc_f), NA_real_)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(surprise = abs(eps - eps_lag) / price_lag)  # Lang & Lundholm's earnings surprise

cs |> select(gvkey, conm, fyear, mv, at, sale, emp, roa, surprise) |> head()
```

### Chunk 2.2 · Frequencies

```{r chunk_2_2}
table(cs$fyear)
table(cs$sic1)
round(prop.table(table(cs$sic1)), 3)      # shares instead of counts
```

**Industries (one-digit SIC):** 0 agriculture · 1 mining & construction · 2–3 manufacturing · 4 transport & utilities · 5 trade · 6 finance · 7–8 services · 9 public administration.

### Chunk 2.3 · A descriptive statistics table

```{r chunk_2_3}
summary(cs$roa)

desc_table <- cs |>
  select(mv, at, sale, emp, roa, surprise) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(N      = sum(!is.na(value)),
            mean   = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd     = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            p1     = quantile(value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
            p25    = quantile(value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            p75    = quantile(value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
            p99    = quantile(value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))

desc_table |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

# Part 3 · Visualisation with ggplot2

`ggplot2` builds a figure in layers: **data** + **aesthetics** (`aes()`: which variable goes on which axis) + **geoms** (the type of plot) + options, connected with `+`.

```         
ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +
  geom_...() +
  labs(...)
```

### Chunk 3.1 · Histograms: raw, log and winsorized

```{r chunk_3_1}

ggplot(cs, aes(x = mv)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(title = "Market value (USD millions)", x = NULL, y = "Firm-years")

ggplot(cs, aes(x = log(mv))) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(title = "Market value (USD millions)", x = "log(MV)", y = "Firm-years")

```

## Winsorizing and truncating

Accounting data almost always contain extreme values: tiny shell companies, data errors, firms in distress.
Two standard ways to limit their influence:

|   | **Winsorizing** | **Truncating** (trimming) |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| What happens | values below the 1st / above the 99th percentile are **replaced** by these percentiles | observations below the 1st / above the 99th percentile are **deleted** |
| Sample size | unchanged | smaller |
| Typical use | continuous variables in regressions (most accounting papers: 1% / 99%) | when extreme values are likely errors or a different population |
| Risk | the capped values are not real values | you may delete exactly the interesting cases (e.g. distressed firms) |

Both are decisions you must **report** (variable, cut-offs, pooled or by year).

### Chunk 3.2 · Two functions

```{r chunk_3_2}
## Test on numbers we know (known inputs!)
winsorize <- function(x, p_low = 0.01, p_high = 0.99) {
  cuts <- quantile(x, probs = c(p_low, p_high), type = 2, na.rm = TRUE) 
  x[x < cuts[1]] <- cuts[1]
  x[x > cuts[2]] <- cuts[2]
}

truncate <- function(x, p_low = 0.01, p_high = 0.99) {
  cuts <- quantile(x, probs = c(p_low, p_high), type = 2, na.rm = TRUE) 
  x[x < cuts[1] | x > cuts[2]] <- NA
  x
}


## Test on numbers we know
test <- c(-1000, 1:99, 5000)
range(winsorize(test))

sum(is.na(truncate(test)))

sum


```

### Chunk 3.3 · Compare raw, winsorized and truncated ROA

```{r chunk_3_3}


```

Even after winsorizing, the lowest values are around −34: the bottom 1% consists of tiny shell companies with almost no assets.
Winsorizing is a technical fix; a **sample choice** (e.g. total assets of at least USD 1 million) is a substantive one — and you must report it.

# Part 4 · Proxies and construct validity

A **proxy** is an observable variable that stands in for a concept we cannot observe directly.
**Construct validity** asks: does the proxy capture the concept — and *only* the concept?

## 4.1 One concept, several proxies: firm size

Lang and Lundholm use **market value** for size.
Others use total assets, sales or employees.
Do they measure the same thing?

### Chunk 4.1 · Correlations between size proxies

```{r chunk_4_1}
## Pearson correlation (raw values) vs. Spearman (ranks)


```

The Pearson correlations of the raw values are driven by a handful of giant firms.
Rank correlations (Spearman) are more robust.

**Task D:** Are the ten "largest" firms the same under each proxy?
Which proxy makes banks (SIC 6) look biggest — and why?

```{r task_D}
## Banks: huge balance sheets, relatively few employees


```

## 4.2 Scaling and extreme values: the earnings surprise

Lang and Lundholm control for the **earnings surprise**: $|EPS_t - EPS_{t-1}| / P_{t-1}$.
Dividing by price makes the measure comparable across firms — but what happens when the price is tiny?

### Chunk 4.2 · Where do the extreme values come from?

```{r chunk_4_2}


```

Three ways to deal with it:

1.  **Winsorize** at 1% / 99% (keeps the order, caps the extremes)
2.  **Require a minimum price**, e.g. $P_{t-1} \geq 1$ USD (changes the sample!)
3.  **Ranks:** Lang and Lundholm convert every variable into its **percentile rank within the industry-year**: $(rank - 1) / (n - 1)$, so the lowest firm gets 0 and the highest 1.

### Chunk 4.3 · Lang & Lundholm's industry-year percentile ranks

```{r chunk_4_3}
## Same concept, three versions: how similar are they?


```

**Task E:** The ranks are almost perfectly correlated with the raw values in Spearman terms — so what do we gain?
And what do we lose when we use ranks?

## 4.3 Measuring disclosure today: the SRN data

Lang and Lundholm measured disclosure with expert ratings.
Today we have machine-readable sustainability reports.
A simple proxy for **disclosure completeness**: the share of the 27 ESRS indicators that SRN found in a firm's report.
